diagnoses.headline: Timing Chain Failure Risk
diagnoses.summary: Rear timing-chain wear that can move from rattle to total engine damage quickly on affected BMW diesels.

overrideCopy.headline: Do not keep driving on a chain-rattle BMW
overrideCopy.body: If the chain slips, the engine can move from repairable noise to full replacement territory in one event.
actions: Avoid restart attempts if the engine has already cut out.
Arrange recovery instead of driving it to a garage.
Inspect chain condition before pricing the rest of the car.

nextSteps: Confirm whether the noise is rear-of-engine chain rattle, not front accessory noise.
Get a specialist to inspect chain stretch before authorising a replacement engine.
Use car value against the replacement range before committing.

diagnoses.headline: EGR Cooler Fire-Risk Fault
diagnoses.summary: Cooler leakage and thermal failure risk on affected diesel BMWs where coolant loss and intake contamination overlap.
diagnoses.evidenceLabel: Safety-critical diesel cooling and emissions path

overrideCopy.headline: Fire-risk cooling fault: recover the car
overrideCopy.body: This is one of the few BMW diesel faults where continued driving is a safety decision, not just a cost decision.
actions: Do not continue driving if there is smoke, coolant smell, or heat warning overlap.
Check campaign history and cooler revision with a BMW specialist.
Inspect for secondary intake contamination before clearing fault codes.

nextSteps: Check whether the car has documented cooler replacement history.
Inspect intake tract and manifold contamination before sign-off.
If overheating happened, compare repair total with engine risk exposure.

diagnoses.headline: Cooling-System Pressure or Expansion Fault
diagnoses.summary: Coolant loss, pressure spikes, or expansion-tank weakness that can escalate into overheating and head damage if ignored.

overrideCopy.headline: Stop before overheating turns into engine damage
overrideCopy.body: A cooling fault caught early is a repair bill. Continued heat cycling can push the car into replacement maths.
actions: Do not keep topping up and driving blind.
Pressure-test the system before replacing random parts.
If temperature has spiked, inspect for secondary head-gasket or block damage.

nextSteps: Find whether the leak is the tank, cap, line, or internal pressure issue.
If the car overheated, widen the inspection before approving parts.
Use the verdict below if replacement costs are now in play.

diagnoses.headline: Valve Stem Seal Wear
diagnoses.summary: Blue smoke after idling or on overrun, usually on older BMW petrol engines where oil control has deteriorated.
nextSteps: Confirm smoke on overrun versus turbo or PCV-related smoke.
Check compression before choosing top-end repair over replacement.
Compare oil-consumption severity against the car's value and intended ownership horizon.

diagnoses.headline: High-Pressure Fuel Pump Failure
diagnoses.summary: Long crank, rail-pressure faults, or sudden power loss where a failing HPFP can strand the car or contaminate the system.

overrideCopy.headline: Fuel pressure fault: avoid a roadside failure
overrideCopy.body: HPFP failure can look like a simple power issue until the car no longer starts or starves itself under load.
actions: Limit driving if the car is dropping pressure or stalling.
Inspect fuel contamination before fitting a replacement pump.
Do not assume injectors are safe until rail health is checked.

nextSteps: Confirm rail-pressure codes and cold-start behavior.
Inspect low-pressure supply side before replacing the HPFP.
If contamination is present, widen the quote to protect injectors.

diagnoses.headline: ZF8HP Mechatronic Fault
diagnoses.summary: Shift logic, engagement, or gearbox warning behavior linked to mechatronic control rather than total transmission failure.
nextSteps: Differentiate control fault from clutch-pack wear before replacing the unit.
Fluid history matters; get gearbox temperature and pressure data.
If the box is otherwise healthy, this often stays in repair territory.

diagnoses.headline: ZF8HP Valve-Body Wear
diagnoses.summary: Flare, lazy engagement, or shift inconsistency caused by valve-body wear rather than complete gearbox failure.
nextSteps: Confirm flare or delay is hydraulic, not software adaptation alone.
Review fluid condition and prior servicing before escalating to replacement.
If clutch damage is absent, repair usually beats replacement on value.

diagnoses.headline: xDrive Transfer Case Wear
diagnoses.summary: Binding, judder, or drivetrain fault behavior tied to transfer-case wear or adaptation issues.
nextSteps: Check tyre circumference mismatch before condemning the transfer case.
Reset adaptations only after mechanical condition is checked.
If gears are damaged, compare replacement against car value before proceeding.

diagnoses.headline: DPF or EGR Restriction
diagnoses.summary: Soot load, repeat regenerations, and intake contamination that can drag performance down and trigger limp mode.
nextSteps: Confirm soot load and differential pressure before replacing emissions hardware.
Short-trip usage and thermostat health usually matter here.
If restriction has already overheated supporting parts, recost before deciding.

diagnoses.headline: Active Steering System Fault
diagnoses.summary: Warning lights, inconsistent assist, or steering behavior caused by active steering electronics or rack-side issues.
nextSteps: Confirm whether the fault is electronic, sensor-based, or rack mechanical wear.
Battery health and coding state can distort diagnosis here.
High repair cost on low-value cars can move this into exit territory.

diagnoses.headline: Crank Pulley / Harmonic Balancer Wear
diagnoses.summary: Idle wobble, accessory vibration, or belt-path movement caused by a deteriorating crank pulley.
nextSteps: Rule out tensioner noise before replacing the damper.
If the belt path has already failed, inspect for secondary front-end damage.
Usually a repair-first diagnosis unless the engine already overheated or lost timing.

diagnoses.headline: VANOS Solenoid Performance Fault
diagnoses.summary: Response loss, timing plausibility codes, or uneven torque delivery from sticky VANOS control hardware.
nextSteps: Check oil condition and service history first.
These faults often repair well without replacement-level spend.
If codes return after replacement, inspect timing correlation and wiring.

diagnoses.headline: Injector Seal Leakage
diagnoses.summary: Misfire, blow-by smell, or smoke linked to leaking injector seats or related sealing issues.
nextSteps: Check whether the issue is only sealing or includes injector failure.
Carbon build-up around the seat can change the labour profile fast.
If compression is healthy, repair is usually the stronger call.

diagnoses.headline: Oil Filter Housing Leak
diagnoses.summary: Front-of-engine oil or coolant leak around the housing, usually repairable if caught before contamination spreads.
nextSteps: Differentiate housing leak from valve cover or front cover seepage.
If coolant and oil mixed, inspect beyond the gasket before pricing.
This normally stays firmly in repair territory when caught early.

diagnoses.headline: Valve Cover Gasket Leak
diagnoses.summary: Oil seepage and smell from the rocker-cover area, often annoying rather than terminal when handled early.
nextSteps: Check whether the cover itself is warped before replacing only the gasket.
Repair quickly if oil is reaching ignition or exhaust-side heat.
This is usually a repair, not a replacement, diagnosis.

diagnoses.headline: Mixed or Unclear BMW Fault Pattern
diagnoses.summary: Your symptoms do not map cleanly to one known fault, so the safest route is specialist diagnosis before parts are priced.
nextSteps: Book diagnosis before ordering parts.
Use the vehicle value and engine option below as planning numbers only.
If multiple systems are involved, widen the budget before deciding.
